How does one SELECT statement travel all the way down to bytes on disk? From a string to pread(2), we'll follow the query engine layer by layer.

The starting point is plain SQL text. Lexing first cuts that string into tokens. The rule is maximal munch: >= is one token, and age30, with no space, is one identifier. Parsing then uses recursive descent and Pratt parsing to build an unresolved AST.

The AST still only represents what was written. It doesn't yet know whether a users table or an age column exists. Binding consults the catalog, and column names become positions (table and column numbers), PostgreSQL's Var nodes. After that, SQL syntax disappears, replaced by a logical plan of Scan, Filter, Join, and friends.

The first improvement is rewriting without changing meaning: split AND and push predicates down to scans. But with OR, NULL, and outer joins, the same transformation may no longer be safe. Next, row counts are estimated from statistics. The histogram gives age > 30 a selectivity of 0.55, or 55,000 of 100,000 rows.

Cost is not time; it is a relative score. One sequential page read is 1.0, then CPU and I/O are added. In the article's example, the same index varies 75-fold in heap I/O cost purely from how well index order matches physical order. For joins, nested loop, merge join, and hash join are compared, and in this example the hash join wins.

With three or more tables, join order matters even more than the join algorithm. System R style dynamic programming keeps only the best plan per subset, shrinking the state space to 2^n. In the article's example, the order as written costs 605,000, while the best order costs 15,000, roughly 40 times cheaper.

At this point, the logical plan commits to a concrete physical plan. This SELECT sequentially scans orders, builds a hash table from users, and joins them. Because of ORDER BY and LIMIT 10, the planner picks a Top-N heap sort instead of sorting everything.

Execution uses the Volcano model: every operator has open, next, and close. A next() call travels downward through the tree, and rows climb back upward. Blocking operators can't emit a first row early: Sort must drain its whole input, HashJoin its build side.

When work_mem is exceeded, different operators degrade in different ways. Sort switches to external merge and degrades gracefully, adding disk I/O on top of comparison cost. Hashing is harsher: it repartitions input into temporary files, so the cost can jump suddenly. In parallel plans, the key is placing Gather, which collects worker rows, as high in the plan tree as possible to reduce shipped rows.

Below the executor, access methods turn logical rows into physical locations. A PostgreSQL TID is a pair of block number and line-pointer number. Every page goes through the buffer pool: hits are reused, misses pick a victim with clock-sweep.

At the bottom, rows live inside 8192-byte slotted pages. Because a TID points to a slot, not a byte offset, a tuple can move within the page without its TID changing. Finally, reading block 4271 becomes pread on fd 42: 8192 bytes at offset 34,988,032.
SQL execution is a chain of transformations, from text to physical I/O. In the article, you can try demos for tokenizing, join order, Volcano execution, spilling, the buffer pool, and page layout.
同じ待ち行列でも、次に何を動かすべきかの正解は1つではありません。CPUからネットワーク、LLM推論まで、目的ごとの枝分かれをたどります。
まず必要なのは、良いスケジュールの定義です。平均を縮めるのか、反応を早めるのか。締切を守る、公平に分ける、能力を使い切る、P99を抑える。目的はしばしば衝突します。

FCFSは到着順に完了まで走らせます。長い仕事の後ろで短い仕事が待たされるコンボイ効果が起き得ます。SJFは全ジョブが同時にそろっていれば、短い仕事を先に選んで平均待ち時間を最小化します。SRTFは残り最短へ切り替えます。理想条件では平均フロー時間を最小にしますが、長い仕事は飢餓し得ます。RRは切替コストと引き換えに、まず全員を一度動かします。MLFQは過去の振る舞いから短い・対話的な仕事を推測します。
締切の枝では、EDFが最も早い絶対締切を持つ仕事を選びます。独立ジョブ、プリエンプション可能な単一CPU、切替コストなしなら、締切を守れるスケジュールがあればEDFも守れます。RMは周期が短いタスクほど高い固定優先度を与えます。公平性ではなく実行可能性の枝です。
比例配分の枝では、重みで正規化した累積処理量が小さい主体を選びます。抽選は確率で配り、ストライドはpassを決定的に進めます。重みが大きいほど進みが遅く、そのぶん頻繁に選ばれます。2026年時点のmainline Linuxでは、通常タスクの既定がEEVDFです。公平な取り分より先行していないタスクのうち、仮想締切が最も早いものを選びます。

ネットワークでは、パケットは送信を始めると途中で細かく割れません。GPS、つまり一般化プロセッサ共有は、各フローを重みに比例して流体のように同時に流す理想モデルです。WFQは仮想完了時刻を、開始時刻公平キューイング、SFQは仮想開始時刻を比べます。この差がLLMルーターで効きます。DRRはタグを使わず、フローを順に回って割当量を配り、使い残しを不足カウンターに持ち越して、ならし定数時間を狙います。
LLMでは入力長は分かっても、出力長は生成終了まで確定しません。max_tokensも上限にすぎないため、SJFやWFQには長さの予測が要ります。プリフィルはプロンプトを並列に処理して計算が重く、デコードは1トークンずつ生成しながらKVキャッシュを読み続けます。外側のルーターでは不可分な仕事でも、エンジン内部の継続的バッチ処理では、デコード反復の境界でバッチを組み替えられます。
無改造のサーバー群の前では、テナントごとのFIFOとメーターを持つSFQが単純です。選ぶのはメーター最小のテナントです。現在のコストは今通すかを決めません。そのコストは、そのテナントが次の番まで待つ長さに効きます。空だったテナントが戻るときは、メーターを少なくとも基準線まで引き上げます。アイドル中の権利を貯めさせません。保証は推定コスト上の投入順序の公平性までで、実測GPU時間ではありません。

For the same queue, there is no single correct answer to what should run next. From CPU scheduling to networks and LLM inference, let's trace how scheduling branches by goal.

The first question is what “good” means: shorter averages, faster first response, or something else. Meeting deadlines, sharing fairly, using all capacity, and lowering P99 often pull in different directions.

FCFS runs jobs in arrival order until completion, but short jobs can pile up behind a long one: the convoy effect. SJF chooses the shortest known job first and minimizes mean waiting time when all jobs are present at once. SRTF switches to the shortest remaining job; ideally it minimizes mean flow time, but long jobs can starve. Round Robin lets every task run soon, at the cost of switching overhead; MLFQ infers short, interactive work from past behavior.

On the deadline branch, EDF selects the ready job with the earliest absolute deadline. With independent jobs, one preemptive CPU, and negligible switching cost, if any schedule can meet the deadlines, EDF can too. RM gives shorter-period tasks higher fixed priority. This branch is about feasibility, not equal service.

In the proportional-share branch, schedulers favor the principal with the least normalized service so far. Lottery uses randomness; Stride advances a deterministic pass more slowly for larger weights, so those tasks are picked more often. As of 2026, mainline Linux uses EEVDF for normal tasks. Among tasks not ahead of their fair share, it picks the earliest virtual deadline.

Networks add a twist: once a packet starts transmitting, it normally cannot be split and interleaved. GPS, Generalized Processor Sharing, is an ideal fluid model serving backlogged flows simultaneously in proportion to their weights. WFQ compares virtual finish tags, while Start-time Fair Queueing, SFQ, compares start tags. That timing shift matters for LLM routers. DRR skips tags: it visits flows in turn, grants a quantum, carries unused credit as deficit, and aims for constant time per packet.

For LLMs, input length is known, but output length is not final until generation ends. max_tokens is only a cap, so SJF or WFQ would need a length predictor. Prefill is parallel and compute-heavy; decode generates one token at a time while reading the KV cache. So a request can be indivisible at the router, yet engine continuous batching can regroup it at every decode iteration.

In front of unmodified servers, SFQ with per-tenant FIFO queues and meters is a simple router policy. Select the tenant with the smallest meter. The current request's cost never decides whether it passes now. It only affects how long that tenant waits for its next turn. When an idle tenant returns, its meter is raised to at least the current baseline. Unused share cannot be banked. The guarantee is admission fairness over estimated cost, not measured GPU time.

If you control the engine, VTC, the Virtual Token Counter from OSDI 2024, gives a different answer. VTC charges each client's counter for input tokens. It adds actual output tokens every decode iteration, and favors the client with the smallest counter. When prefix locality also matters, DLPM comes from a 2025 preprint. It favors prefix matches while a per-client quantum lasts, relaxing fair order in a controlled way. The 2025 Equinox preprint argues that one token counter cannot capture latency, throughput, and GPU utilization.
The article includes interactive CPU and LLM demos, so you can run the policies yourself and see the differences.
ベクトルデータベースは、どうやって似ている文書を一瞬で探すのでしょうか。全探索からIVF、PQ、HNSW、DiskANNまで、近似最近傍探索の中身をたどります。
埋め込みは、テキストや画像を固定次元の実数ベクトルに写します。意味が近いものほど、空間上でも近い点として並びます。検索とは、クエリ点の近くにある点を探す幾何の問題です。
ただし次元数は1000を超えることが普通です。OpenAI text-embedding-3-smallは1536次元、largeは3072次元です。高次元では距離が集中し、kd-treeのような分割も効きにくくなります。だから実用では、真の上位k件を完全には求めない近似探索、ANNで、95%以上の再現率を狙います。
ベースラインはFlat、つまり全ベクトルとの距離を測る方法です。計算量はO(Nd)。Nが100万、dが1024なら、1クエリで4GBを走査します。ANNの工夫は、見るベクトル数を減らすか、距離計算を軽くするかです。
IVFは空間をセントロイドごとのセルに分け、候補を減らします。構築時はk-meansでnlist個のセントロイドを作り、各点を最も近いセルへ入れます。検索時はクエリに近いセルをnprobe個だけ開き、その中だけを走査します。ただし正解が開かなかったセルにあれば、再現率は落ちます。
PQは、長いベクトルを短い整数コードへ圧縮します。1024次元を64個に分け、各部分を、256個の代表ベクトルを持つコードブックで最も近いものの番号に置き換えます。4096バイトのfloat32ベクトルは、64バイトのコードになります、64倍の圧縮です。検索ではクエリとコードブックの距離表を先に作り、あとは表の値を足すだけです。
HNSWは、似ているベクトル同士を友達リンクで結ぶ多層グラフです。上の層は疎な世界地図、一番下の層は全点を含む市街地図です。検索は上層で貪欲に方向を決め、Layer 0ではefSearch本の候補を同時に広げます。各点の最大リンク数Mを大きくすれば再現率は上がりますが、リンクのメモリも増えます。
HNSWは全データがRAMに載る前提です。10億本の1024次元float32ベクトルは、生で4TBになります。DiskANNはVamanaグラフと元のベクトルをSSDに置き、RAMにはPQで圧縮したベクトルだけを置きます。1ホップが4KBランダムリードなので、長距離エッジでホップ数を減らします。
実システムでは、公開済み文書だけ、特定テナントだけ、というフィルタも必要です。後から絞るpost-filterは簡単ですが、通過率が低いと上位k件が空になりがちです。先に絞るpre-filterは小さな集合には強い一方、ANNの速さを捨てる場面があります。通過率が中くらいの難しい領域では、Qdrantのようにフィルタ可能なHNSWで接続性を守ります。
本番の選択は、データ量、メモリ予算、更新頻度、再現率目標で決まります。小規模ならFlat、RAMが潤沢ならHNSW、メモリ制約が強ければIVFPQ、10億規模ならDiskANNです。運用ではRecall@k、QPS、p99レイテンシ、構築時間、インデックスサイズを見ます。BM25とベクトル検索の結果をRRFで融合し、cross-encoderで再ランキングする構成も一般的です。
ベクトルDBは魔法の箱ではなく、高次元空間に拡張された索引の集合です。記事では、PQやHNSWのインタラクティブデモと、実装上の落とし穴まで解説しています。続きは、vector-database-internalsの記事で確認してください。
How does a vector database find similar documents in an instant? From brute force to IVF, PQ, HNSW, and DiskANN, let's trace the machinery behind approximate nearest neighbor search.

An embedding maps text or images into fixed-dimensional real-valued vectors. Items with similar meaning become nearby points in that space. Search becomes a geometric problem: find the points nearest to the query point.

But the dimensionality is commonly above one thousand. OpenAI text-embedding-3-small has 1536 dimensions; text-embedding-3-large has 3072. In high dimensions, distances concentrate, and structures like kd-trees stop pruning effectively. So production systems relax to ANN: return most of the true top-k, often targeting 95% recall or higher.

The baseline is Flat search: measure the distance to every stored vector. Its cost is O(Nd). With N equal to one million and d equal to 1024, one query streams 4 GB. ANN speeds this up in two ways: visit fewer vectors, or make each distance computation cheaper.

IVF reduces candidates by partitioning the space into centroid-owned cells. At build time, k-means creates nlist centroids, and each point goes to its nearest cell. At query time, IVF opens only the nprobe cells closest to the query and scans inside them. If the true neighbor sits in a cell you did not open, recall drops.

PQ compresses long vectors into short integer codes. For 1024 dimensions, split into 64 parts, then replace each part with the ID of its nearest entry in a 256-entry codebook. A 4096-byte float32 vector becomes a 64-byte code: 64× compression. During search, precompute query-to-codebook distance tables, then score each vector by summing table entries.

HNSW is a layered graph where similar vectors are connected by neighbor links. The upper layers are sparse world maps; the bottom layer is the dense street map containing every point. Search greedily descends through upper layers, then expands an efSearch-wide beam on Layer 0. Increasing M, the maximum links per node, improves recall but also increases link memory.

HNSW assumes the whole index fits in RAM. One billion 1024-dimensional float32 vectors take 4 TB before indexing overhead. DiskANN keeps its Vamana graph and full vectors on SSD, with only PQ-compressed vectors in RAM. Because one hop is a 4 KB random read, long-range edges are used to reduce the number of hops.

Real systems also need filters: only published documents, or only one tenant. Post-filtering is simple, but when few items pass the filter, the final top-k can come back empty. Pre-filtering works for tiny subsets, but sometimes throws away the speed advantage of ANN. In the messy middle, where a moderate share passes, systems like Qdrant preserve connectivity with a filterable HNSW graph.

In production, the choice depends on N, memory budget, update rate, and recall target. For small N, use Flat; with enough RAM, HNSW; under memory pressure, IVFPQ; at billion scale, DiskANN. Operationally, watch Recall@k, QPS, p99 latency, build time, and index size. Hybrid pipelines often fuse BM25 and vector results with RRF, then re-rank them with a cross-encoder.

A vector DB is not magic; it is a set of indexing ideas extended into high-dimensional space. The article goes deeper, with interactive demos for PQ and HNSW and the implementation pitfalls to watch for. Read the full vector-database-internals article for the complete walkthrough.
